questions.question: Maven vs Gradle vs Bazel — which build tool and when?
questions.title: Maven vs Gradle vs Bazel: When to Pick Each Build Tool
questions.direct_answer: Maven wins for standard Spring/Jakarta EE projects where convention-over-configuration is a feature — simple, predictable, massive plugin ecosystem, easy onboarding. Gradle wins when builds need flexibility — multi-project, custom logic, Android, polyglot (Kotlin/Java/Scala), or you want incremental builds and build cache for speed. Bazel wins for monorepos at scale — hermetic, reproducible, fine-grained caching, multi-language, but heavyweight setup that pays off only past a certain size.

interviewer_intent.testing: Build tool selection across project size, ecosystem, and reproducibility needs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking Bazel for a small Spring project just because Google uses it — the setup overhead is enormous and unjustified at small scale
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss build cache and incremental compilation as the dividing line, hermetic builds for supply chain security, and the cost curve of each tool by repo size

sections.title: Three Tools Solving the Same Problem at Different Scales
sections.content:
All three compile, test, and package JVM code. The differences emerge at the edges — build speed at scale, custom logic flexibility, multi-language support, and reproducibility guarantees.

**Maven** is the original opinionated build tool: XML-based POMs, fixed lifecycle (validate → compile → test → package → install → deploy), declarative dependency management, and a vast plugin ecosystem (Spring Boot plugin, surefire, failsafe, jacoco, etc.). The strength is convention — any Java engineer can read a POM and understand the build. The weakness is rigidity: when you need to do something off-script (custom code generation, multi-step packaging logic), Maven plugins become painful.

**Gradle** uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL for build scripts. It's much more flexible — you can write actual code in your build, define custom tasks, integrate non-JVM languages, and leverage incremental builds + a remote build cache. The trade-off is build scripts that can become opaque or non-portable. Gradle is the standard for Android, multi-project builds, and any project where build performance matters.

**Bazel** (Google's open-source build system, derived from Blink) is a different beast: hermetic builds (every action's inputs are explicit), fine-grained dependency graphs, distributed remote execution, and content-addressable caching. It supports Java, Kotlin, Go, C++, Python, Rust, Swift, and more in one build. The cost is heavyweight setup — BUILD files everywhere, WORKSPACE for dependency declarations, and a steep learning curve. Pays off massively in monorepos with many languages and many engineers; massively over-engineered for a 5-person Spring team.

sections.title: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Maven | Gradle | Bazel |
|--------|-------|--------|-------|
| **Build script** | XML (pom.xml) | Groovy or Kotlin DSL | Starlark (BUILD.bazel) |
| **Configuration model** | Convention over configuration | Convention + flexible DSL | Explicit dependency graph |
| **Incremental builds** | Limited (full phase recompile) | Yes — task-level + compilation | Yes — fine-grained file-level |
| **Build cache** | Local (~/.m2) only | Local + remote cache | Local + remote + remote execution |
| **Multi-language** | Java/Kotlin/Scala via plugins | Java/Kotlin/Scala/Groovy/Android | Java/Kotlin/Go/C++/Python/Rust/Swift |
| **Hermetic builds** | No | Partial | Yes (sandboxed execution) |
| **Learning curve** | Low | Medium | High |
| **Build performance at scale** | Slow (no incremental) | Fast (incremental + cache) | Fastest (parallel + remote exec) |
| **Plugin ecosystem** | Massive (Apache + 3rd party) | Large | Smaller (Bazel-specific rules) |
| **IDE support** | Excellent | Excellent | Good (less polished) |
| **Best for** | Standard Spring/Jakarta projects | Android, multi-module, complex builds | Monorepos, multi-language, scale |
| **Examples** | Most Spring apps, Apache projects | Android (default), Gradle plugins | Google, Uber, Pinterest, Dropbox |

sections.title: Decision Tree: Picking the Right Tool
sections.content:
**Pick Maven when:**
- Standard Spring Boot or Jakarta EE microservice with no special build needs
- Team is more comfortable with declarative XML than DSL code
- You want maximum predictability — every Maven project looks the same
- You're building a library to publish to Maven Central (Maven is the default and best-supported path)
- Build performance is fine because the project is small (under ~100k LOC)
- Examples: most Spring microservices, Apache projects, mature enterprise codebases

**Pick Gradle when:**
- You're building Android (Gradle is the default and only well-supported choice)
- You have a multi-project build with many modules and want incremental builds
- You need custom build logic that XML can't express cleanly
- You want a remote build cache to share artifacts across the team and CI (massive speedup at scale)
- Polyglot project: Java + Kotlin + Scala in one build
- Examples: Android apps, Spring Boot apps in companies like LinkedIn and Netflix, large multi-module Java codebases

**Pick Bazel when:**
- You have a monorepo with hundreds of modules in multiple languages
- You need hermetic, reproducible builds for supply chain security or compliance
- You want fine-grained dependency tracking and remote execution to make a 1-hour build run in 5 minutes
- You have a dedicated build infrastructure team to maintain it
- Examples: Google (where it originated), Uber, Stripe, Pinterest

**Anti-pattern**: adopting Bazel for a small project because of "future scale." The setup cost is real and immediate; the benefit only materializes once you have many engineers and many modules. Migrate when the pain justifies the cost, not preemptively.

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Common Mistakes
sections.content:
**Maven's plugin escape hatch is also its Achilles' heel.** When you need custom logic, you write a plugin in Java, package it, and reference it in the POM. This works but creates a cycle of plugins-for-plugins. Gradle lets you write the logic inline.

**Gradle's flexibility is also its risk.** A build script that started as 50 lines grows to 500 lines of cryptic Groovy. The Kotlin DSL helps (better IDE support, type checking), but discipline matters. Use convention plugins to share logic across modules.

**Build cache value scales with team size.** A solo developer rebuilding alone gets some speedup from Gradle's local cache. A team of 50 with a remote cache (Gradle Enterprise, Bazel Remote Cache, or self-hosted) sees order-of-magnitude speedups because someone's already built that exact change.

**Bazel's hermetic builds are amazing but constraining.** Tools like `wget` or `curl` in build steps don't work in a sandbox. You declare every input explicitly. This is powerful for reproducibility but forces a different way of thinking. Teams transitioning to Bazel often spend months re-architecting their build process.

**Bazel and the JVM ecosystem.** While Bazel supports Java well, its JVM ecosystem (Maven Central integration, Spring Boot, etc.) is less mature than Maven/Gradle. `rules_jvm_external` helps but is more friction than `mvn install`.

**Migration cost is brutal.** Migrating from Maven to Gradle is doable (Gradle has a `gradle init --type pom` converter). Migrating to Bazel is a multi-quarter project. Pick once, change rarely.

**Don't trust 'this is faster' claims without measuring.** Build performance depends on your specific code, machines, network, and cache hit rate. Measure with your project; don't extrapolate from blog benchmarks.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Maven** — convention-over-configuration XML; vast plugin ecosystem; default for Spring/Jakarta EE projects; slow at scale (no incremental builds)
- **Gradle** — flexible DSL (Groovy/Kotlin); incremental builds + remote cache; default for Android; best for multi-module + complex builds
- **Bazel** — hermetic, fine-grained, multi-language; massive scale (Google, Uber); heavyweight setup; only justified by monorepo size and engineer count
- **Build cache scales with team** — a solo dev sees modest gains; a team of 50 with remote cache sees order-of-magnitude speedups
- **Migration is expensive** — Maven → Gradle is doable; → Bazel is a multi-quarter rearchitecture; pick once and stick with it
- **Anti-pattern**: adopting Bazel preemptively — setup cost is real now, payoff only at scale; let pain justify the migration

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
All three compile, test, and package JVM code. The differences emerge at the edges — speed at scale, flexibility for custom logic, multi-language support, and reproducibility.

**Maven — the convention-over-configuration default**
- XML-based pom.xml with a fixed lifecycle: validate, compile, test, package, install, deploy
- Massive plugin ecosystem: Spring Boot plugin, surefire, failsafe, jacoco — most things have an existing plugin
- Strength: any Java engineer can read a Maven project and understand the build; high predictability
- Weakness: when you need custom logic that doesn't fit a plugin, the workaround is painful; no incremental builds, so large projects are slow
- Best for: standard Spring or Jakarta EE microservices, libraries published to Maven Central, projects under ~100k lines of code

**Gradle — the flexible DSL with build cache**
- Build scripts in Groovy or Kotlin DSL; you can write actual code, define custom tasks, integrate non-JVM languages
- Incremental builds at the task level plus a remote build cache that can be shared across team and CI — huge speedup once you scale past a single developer
- Default for Android (the only well-supported choice); strong for multi-module Java projects
- Trade-off: build scripts can grow into 500-line Groovy beasts; discipline and convention plugins matter
- Best for: Android, multi-module builds, polyglot projects, anywhere build performance is important

**Bazel — the monorepo scale-out option**
- Originated at Google; hermetic builds where every action's inputs are explicit; sandboxed execution; content-addressable caching; remote execution
- Supports Java, Kotlin, Go, C++, Python, Rust, Swift in one build — the only good option for a true polyglot monorepo
- Massive setup cost: BUILD files everywhere, WORKSPACE for deps, steep learning curve, JVM ecosystem less polished than Maven/Gradle
- Pays off in repos with hundreds of modules and many engineers; over-engineered for a 5-person team
- Examples: Google, Uber, Stripe, Pinterest, Dropbox

**The dividing lines**
- Build cache value scales with team size — solo dev gets modest gains, team of 50 with remote cache gets order-of-magnitude speedups
- Hermetic builds matter for supply chain security — reproducible builds let you prove what artifacts were built from what source
- Migration cost is brutal — Maven to Gradle is doable, but moving to Bazel is a multi-quarter rearchitecture; pick once

**The anti-pattern**
- Adopting Bazel for a small project because of "future scale" — the setup cost is real and immediate; the benefit only materializes at scale; migrate when pain justifies cost, not preemptively

**The default recommendation**
- New Spring service: Maven for simplicity
- Multi-module enterprise codebase, Android, or build performance matters: Gradle
- 100+ engineers in a polyglot monorepo: Bazel, with a dedicated build platform team
